title: Can the UK stay on track for net zero?
label: 9 September 2026 · UK climate progress
summary: MPs questioned the Climate Change Committee, the UK's independent climate adviser, about whether Government policies are strong enough to meet national and international emissions targets. The witnesses reported substantial progress in renewable electricity and electric vehicles, but warned that expensive electricity, slow heat pump installations, delayed infrastructure and weak plans for farming and industry could undermine further progress. They questioned the Government's reliance on technologies that remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, especially where funding and delivery plans remain uncertain. MPs challenged the costs of the transition, its effects on manufacturing, the growth of energy-hungry data centres and the lack of timely independent advice on Heathrow expansion. The central message was that the UK has credible routes to net zero, but the Government needs faster action in several areas, clearer plans for risky technologies and alternatives ready if its assumptions prove wrong.

glossary.definition: An independent body that advises UK governments on climate change and assesses their progress towards legally binding targets.
A legal limit on the total greenhouse gases the UK can emit over a five-year period.
Reaching a point where greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere are balanced by gases removed from it.
A heating system that uses electricity to move heat from outside into a building, usually using less energy than a conventional boiler.
Land containing partly decayed vegetation that stores large amounts of carbon but can release it when drained or damaged.
An electricity price plan that charges different rates depending on when electricity is used.
The regulator responsible for overseeing Britain's gas and electricity markets and protecting energy consumers.
Greenhouse gases released within a country's borders, rather than emissions caused overseas by producing goods it imports.
Technologies designed to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and store it for a very long time.
The network of cables, substations and other equipment that carries electricity from power stations to users.
UK rules requiring manufacturers to ensure that an increasing proportion of the new vehicles they sell are zero-emission.
A heat pump that warms or cools indoor air directly, rather than heating water for radiators.
A gas that can be used as fuel, potentially with low emissions if it is produced using suitable low-carbon methods.
Technology that captures carbon dioxide and stores it, usually underground, to stop it entering the atmosphere.
A system that charges certain imports according to the emissions produced in making them, accounting for differences in countries' carbon prices.
Aircraft fuel made from alternatives to conventional fossil oil, such as waste materials or captured carbon dioxide.
An international aviation scheme that requires airlines to address certain emissions by buying approved carbon credits.
Certificates representing claimed emissions reductions or removals, which organisations can buy to compensate for emissions.
The total greenhouse gases associated with a person, product or country's activities, including emissions from goods made elsewhere.

chapters.title: Climate progress and public accountability
chapters.takeaway: UK emissions have fallen substantially, but the Government's plans leave important gaps, while delays in independent advice are making parliamentary scrutiny harder.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Your committee is supposed to help Parliament hold the Government to account on climate change. Yet you've taken months to prepare advice on Heathrow expansion, and you're publishing it after the public consultation has closed. How can Parliament and the public properly scrutinise the proposals without seeing your assessment?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: I understand the frustration. We're a very small organisation with legally required reports to produce on fixed deadlines, including major work on climate risks this year. We also had a change of chair. We couldn't complete this additional request any earlier, although we've continued discussing aviation with Government officials throughout.

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: It's also a substantial piece of analysis. We were asked to look beyond the Heathrow proposal itself and assess how aviation emissions fit with the UK's carbon budgets and its net zero target. That required new calculations.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But Parliament will have only 21 sitting days to decide whether to approve the final policy statement once it's presented. The Government could change the proposals following consultation. Will you assess that final version, rather than leave MPs relying on advice about an earlier draft?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: We'll publish our assessment and make ourselves available to MPs, including through the Transport Committee. We don't currently intend to carry out another round of modelling. We believe the advice we're producing will give Parliament useful information for considering the proposals, though I recognise the timing is difficult.

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: We were specifically commissioned to assess the draft and recommend changes where necessary. We don't have an automatic legal duty to assess national policy statements. Our published advice will fulfil the request we've received.

turns.speaker: Dr Roz Savage
turns.text: Turning to the wider picture, what should the new Prime Minister and Secretaries of State prioritise over the coming year to keep the UK on track with its climate commitments?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: There's real progress. UK emissions have roughly halved since 2008. Around a quarter of new car sales are electric, renewable electricity generation has reached record levels, and peatland restoration increased by 24%. But the Government's current policies don't deliver its international emissions pledge for 2030 and only just meet its sixth carbon budget. Around 60% of the policies have either credible plans or relatively limited risks. We particularly need faster adoption of electric cars and heat pumps.

turns.speaker: Dr Roz Savage
turns.text: What about the Environment Secretary? What should happen with nature, farming and the land?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Peatland restoration is improving, particularly in Scotland, but tree planting has fallen sharply. The Government needs to increase planting substantially to meet its own ambitions. New policies on land use and sustainable farming are welcome because they can help farmers make these changes, but much more investment and sustained support will be needed.

chapters.title: Cheaper electricity and the risks in Government plans
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses argued that reducing electricity costs and using proven technologies sooner could save money and make climate targets more achievable.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: The Prime Minister has temporarily removed VAT from household electricity. How much difference will that make, and what else is needed?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Ofgem estimates that without the VAT cut, typical bills on variable tariffs would have been about £45 higher. But rising wholesale prices have reduced the benefit. Electricity still costs about 3.3 times as much as gas per unit. We need that gap to narrow so efficient electric heating becomes financially attractive. The Government could move charges currently added to electricity bills into general taxation or elsewhere. Grants and affordable finance are also needed to help people pay for equipment.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: There's also renewed discussion about North Sea drilling, including Rosebank and Jackdaw. Would more production help emissions, energy prices or energy security?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Our carbon budgets count emissions from extracting oil and gas within UK territory, but not all emissions when that fuel is eventually burned. We haven't been asked to assess new drilling specifically. North Sea production is expected to decline by about 93% by 2050 even with new fields, so communities dependent on it need plans for jobs and skills. And because oil and gas prices are set internationally, more UK drilling isn't a reliable way to cut household bills. Reducing our dependence on those fuels is more effective.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: The Government wants to rely more heavily on developing technologies, rather than changing how people travel or heat their homes. What risks does that create?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Using a different approach from ours isn't necessarily wrong. But the Government expects engineered removals to account for about 17% of its emissions reduction between 2031 and 2037. It also assumes benefits from artificial intelligence without fully considering the extra emissions AI could cause. The Government needs clear progress checks and backup measures if technologies don't arrive quickly enough. Those could include faster electrification, more public transport use and additional waste reduction.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: Does delaying investment make the transition more expensive? And which parts of Government are doing well or badly?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Delays mean households miss savings they could already be making. Our analysis suggests that every £1 spent on reaching net zero brings benefits worth about £2.20 to £4.10, even under less favourable assumptions. Electricity generation has been a major success, with emissions down 82% since 2008. But heat pump installations are growing too slowly. The Environment Department has made progress on peatland but not woodland. We also need more attention to heating and cooling public buildings.

chapters.title: The electricity network and the rise of AI
chapters.takeaway: The UK needs a stronger, more flexible electricity network, while rapidly growing data centre demand raises questions about energy supplies, costs and emissions.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Government wants clean electricity by 2030, but your advice says the grid should be strengthened enough to meet needs through to 2050. Could rushing the work now mean having to rebuild parts of it later?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: We need to expand the grid quickly, particularly so factories can switch to electricity. But it must also cope with future demand and more extreme weather. We're already seeing wind farms being told to reduce generation because the network can't carry all their electricity. We need stronger cables, more energy storage and better use of batteries. The network also needs to withstand the hotter conditions expected as the climate changes.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: Data centres are asking for extraordinary amounts of electricity. Connection requests have reportedly reached around 80 gigawatts, compared with a UK winter peak demand of 45 gigawatts. Have your forecasts accounted for that growth? Could data centres take electricity and grid connections needed by homes and industry?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: We used National Grid's highest estimate for future data centre development and allowed additional room for demand growth. I'm reasonably confident our overall electricity forecasts are on the right scale. But deciding which projects get connected, and where data centres can access enough electricity and water, involves Government choices. It's still uncertain how many proposed developments will actually happen.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: Some data centres aren't waiting for clean electricity connections. They're planning to generate their own power using fossil fuels. If that happens on a large scale, couldn't it seriously undermine the UK's carbon budgets?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Large amounts of additional fossil fuel generation would potentially affect the emissions figures we assess. But the Climate Change Committee hasn't yet formed a formal view on these developments, so I can't give you a firm conclusion. We're examining the issue and will consider its implications in future work. Decisions about how data centres are built and supplied with energy ultimately belong to Government.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: There's also been little visible progress on the Government's proposed service to speed up grid connections for major projects. Do you think it has adequate plans to identify and respond to delays?

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: We've consistently recommended that the Government regularly check which parts of its plans are falling behind and prepare alternatives. From what we've seen publicly, those arrangements aren't in place. Over a period of many years, some measures will inevitably progress faster than others, so monitoring and backup plans are essential.

turns.speaker: Sammy Wilson
turns.text: But building the grid faster costs money, and that cost goes on people's electricity bills. Aren't you making electricity more expensive just when you want everyone to start using more of it?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Yes, network investment increases bills in the short term, and that must be taken seriously. But our calculations include those costs and still show that an electricity-based energy system can be cheaper overall. We estimate it could avoid around £30 billion a year in wasted energy. Without the necessary network, factories, car chargers and other equipment can't use electricity efficiently. How the initial costs are shared between households, businesses and taxpayers is a decision for policymakers.

chapters.title: Electric cars: progress, prices and pressure on manufacturers
chapters.takeaway: Electric vehicle sales are growing strongly, but MPs disagreed over whether Government sales requirements support the industry's future or place too much pressure on manufacturers.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: Electric cars seem to be one area of good progress. What would happen if the Government weakened the zero-emission vehicle mandate, which requires manufacturers to sell an increasing share of electric vehicles?

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: Significant weakening would very likely make the UK's 2030 international climate pledge harder to meet. Electric vehicles account for roughly a fifth of the emissions reductions in the Government's plan to 2030. The rules have worked so far, with manufacturers meeting their obligations using the flexibility already allowed. One worthwhile change would be to stop giving plug-in hybrid cars more credit for cutting emissions than the evidence supports.

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: There are now more than two million electric cars on UK roads, and recently they've accounted for around 30% of new sales. Their extra purchase cost compared with petrol cars fell from 24% to 16% over a year, and we expect broadly equal purchase prices within two years. They're already generally cheaper to run, particularly when charged at home. Slowing the transition could delay those savings and make later climate targets harder.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: What about the new electric vehicle road tax, and the fact that charging points are much easier to find in some areas than others?

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: We haven't found evidence that the new tax is discouraging buyers, but we haven't studied it specifically. Charging access does vary considerably. London and Scotland are doing relatively well, while Northern Ireland is much further behind. Government should track whether that affects electric car sales locally and make the new tax arrangements as straightforward as possible.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: What practical changes would make electric cars more attractive, especially for people who can't charge at home?

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: Home charging can save drivers around £450 to £1,600 a year, depending on use. But our calculations show no running-cost saving for people relying on public chargers. We need more affordable, slower street chargers where people can leave cars overnight, better access to cheap electricity rates and consideration of reducing VAT on public charging. That rate is 20%, compared with the temporary 0% rate on household electricity. Any tax cut should reach drivers rather than simply increase charging companies' profits.

turns.speaker: Sammy Wilson
turns.text: You're presenting a very positive picture, but manufacturers have been heavily discounting cars to meet the mandate. Industry figures we've heard suggest enormous costs, while thousands of jobs are threatened at Jaguar Land Rover. Chinese manufacturers are also taking more of the UK market. How long can the industry withstand this pressure? And how will the Government replace fuel tax revenue as petrol and diesel sales decline?

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: Manufacturers are discounting petrol cars too, and competition is putting pressure on prices. More than three-quarters of vehicles made in the UK are exported, mainly to markets such as Europe that also have strong electric vehicle targets. Even if electric cars faced taxes comparable to current fuel duty, their efficiency would still give home-charging drivers running-cost savings. Government revenue is a separate challenge that could be addressed through future taxation.

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: My understanding is that the Jaguar Land Rover redundancies are partly linked to a cyberattack, not simply the vehicle mandate. The bigger issue is that manufacturers worldwide are learning to make cheaper electric cars. British manufacturers need to compete in that market. We believe the mandate helps encourage the necessary investment, although the transition should be made manageable for industry. The future looks increasingly electric, even if petrol vehicles are often cheaper to buy today.

chapters.title: Heating homes without leaving people behind
chapters.takeaway: Heat pumps could cut emissions and household costs, but high electricity prices, installation expenses and shortages of trained workers remain major obstacles.

turns.speaker: Sarah Gibson
turns.text: Millions of homes have poor heating, and the previous Government-backed home improvement scheme had serious problems with badly carried out installations. How can the new warm homes funding avoid repeating those mistakes and help low-income households?

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: The new funding is important for insulation and replacing gas or oil boilers with heat pumps. But installations grew by only 7% last year, compared with 56% the year before. The Government's warm homes ambitions require growth of around 37% a year. Installations in low-income homes have actually fallen. We're concerned that unclear replacement funding could cause further declines.

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: Any new scheme needs proper consumer protection. Installers should be trained, qualified and independently certified. Households must understand what equipment they're being offered, what installation involves and who can resolve problems. Funding should also consider combining heat pumps with insulation, solar panels and batteries where appropriate, so low-income families can benefit from lower running costs.

turns.speaker: Sarah Gibson
turns.text: One cheaper option is an air-to-air heat pump. I've seen installations costing around £8,000 rather than £20,000 for some water-based systems. These weren't supported by previous grants. Could including them help people who can't afford more expensive heating systems?

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: Yes, extending grants to air-to-air systems is positive. They can also cool homes in hot weather. But at present, we understand that no installers have the necessary certification for these installations under the boiler upgrade grant. That needs fixing. Once qualified installers are available, people should be able to access a £2,500 grant, with further support potentially available for low-income households.

turns.speaker: Sarah Gibson
turns.text: People often replace their heating only when their boiler breaks. If they urgently need a replacement, won't they simply choose another gas boiler because it's quicker?

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: That's a major risk. We need a system where people can get low-carbon heating installed quickly when an old boiler fails. Homeowners renovating should consider whether their pipes, radiators, hot water storage and outdoor space will accommodate a future heat pump. Government and industry also need simpler quotations, more standard installation arrangements and many more trained installers.

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Familiarity matters too. About a quarter of newly built homes now have heat pumps, which should help people become comfortable with them. Government could also do much more in hospitals, schools and other public buildings. Installing low-carbon heating and cooling there would reduce emissions and demonstrate how these systems work.

turns.speaker: Sarah Gibson
turns.text: A housing association has told me its lenders won't allow solar panels on certain roofs because of financing restrictions. Have you encountered barriers like that? It could prevent tenants from getting the full savings from a heat pump.

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: We haven't examined that specific lending issue. But not every home can have solar panels, batteries or a time-of-use tariff. That's why making electricity cheaper across the board is so important. People should be able to save money with a heat pump even if they can't install extra equipment.

chapters.title: Industry, jobs and emissions beyond UK borders
chapters.takeaway: Industry needs affordable electricity and long-term investment plans, while the witnesses cautioned against assuming that falling UK emissions simply mean pollution and jobs have moved overseas.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: British manufacturers still face very high electricity prices. Existing discounts don't appear to have persuaded many companies to replace fossil fuel equipment with electric alternatives. Should the Government go further, or try something different?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: It needs to do both. Discounts have brought electricity prices to roughly twice gas prices for an initial group of around 500 companies, which makes switching more attractive. Another group receives smaller discounts. But cheap electricity alone isn't enough. Factories need help paying for new machinery, reliable grid connections, skilled workers and clear long-term plans. Removing support schemes for industrial investment makes that more difficult. The experience at Port Talbot shows why major industries need a planned transition rather than uncertainty about closures and replacements.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: More than half of the UK's overall carbon footprint now comes from imported goods and services. Could falling emissions at home partly reflect manufacturing moving abroad, taking jobs with it?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: It's important to distinguish emissions produced in the UK from emissions associated with what British people buy. We track both. But we haven't found convincing evidence that UK climate policy has caused a large shift of emissions overseas. Domestic emissions have fallen by about half since 2008 while the economic value produced by manufacturing has grown. The kinds of goods Britain makes have changed, often towards higher-value products, and that change began before the Climate Change Act. Other countries are also developing cleaner industries.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: What about hydrogen? The Government hasn't awarded contracts under its second funding round, even though applications closed two years ago. Does that threaten industrial progress?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: We're concerned about the delays and don't know the reason for them. We estimate that around 60% of industrial emissions could be addressed through switching to electricity. Other processes will need technologies such as hydrogen and carbon capture and storage, particularly where electricity alone can't do the job. Those industries need predictable funding decisions and timetables so companies can invest with confidence.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: The Government also expects carbon capture and storage to expand rapidly. Is that realistic, or are we already too late?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: The technology is real, with around 70 plants operating internationally, so including it in a climate plan is reasonable. More than £9 billion of Government funding is welcome. But the Government is depending on a faster expansion than we assumed, especially between 2031 and 2037. It needs a clear schedule, future funding commitments, ways for projects to earn money and alternatives if development is slower than expected.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: We've discussed UK emissions and emissions from imported products. But what about emissions caused when British investors finance businesses overseas? Should those be counted too?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: That's an interesting question, but it falls outside our legal responsibilities. We assess territorial emissions because Governments can directly regulate activities inside their borders. Overseas emissions also matter, but addressing them involves trade, international agreements and decisions by other countries. I think territorial accounting remains a practical basis for national climate law.

turns.speaker: Sarah Gibson
turns.text: Construction is a good example of why overseas emissions matter. A building's carbon footprint includes making and transporting materials, not just the energy it uses once occupied. Shouldn't we account for that?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: We do track emissions associated with imported materials, even though they aren't included in the UK's legally binding territorial totals. Policymakers can act through purchasing rules, trade policy and measures such as the planned carbon border adjustment mechanism. Emissions from materials made in Britain are already counted, although they appear under industries such as cement production rather than building use. The wider purchasing decisions are mainly for Government and businesses.

chapters.title: Aviation, cleaner fuels and the cost of flying
chapters.takeaway: Cleaner aviation fuels are beginning to grow, but their future supply is uncertain, and the witnesses argued that flying should expand only as emissions-reducing technologies become available.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: Sustainable aviation fuel has increased only slightly, from 2.2% to 2.5% of fuel use. The Government wants 10% by 2030. How can it speed up production of more advanced fuels?

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: The current share meets the initial requirement, but almost all of it comes from an early type of fuel made using oils and fats. The longer-term transition needs more advanced fuels made from other biological materials or captured carbon. These are harder to produce at scale and finance. Government should maintain its requirements for the different fuel types and bring forward investment contracts if possible. Those contracts would give producers more confidence that they'll have buyers.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: Should the Government widen its fuel requirements to cover aviation emissions more generally, rather than concentrating on particular fuels?

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: That comes close to the advice we're preparing for publication next week on Heathrow and wider aviation policy. I can't discuss our conclusions before they're published.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: The Government also expects airlines to use international carbon credits through CORSIA. But there's uncertainty about whether enough reliable credits will exist, and Ministers don't appear to have plans to limit flying if cleaner technology falls behind. How credible is that approach?

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: There are real concerns about the quality and availability of credits, and the current international scheme doesn't extend beyond 2035. Government needs strict rules and plans for those risks. We think emissions from flying should ultimately be balanced by removing carbon dioxide permanently, rather than relying on short-lived measures. We don't think the next carbon budget needs international credits because domestic action could achieve it, although circumstances could change.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: But passenger demand has already grown by 7%. Doesn't that suggest flights could keep increasing, especially if airports expand?

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: Much of the recent increase reflects recovery after the pandemic, and aviation emissions didn't continue rising this year, which was reassuring. Our advice assumes demand stays roughly at today's level until 2035, then grows if cleaner fuels and permanent carbon removals develop sufficiently. If they don't, growth may need to be restrained. We also think the cost of reducing aviation emissions should be reflected in ticket prices. That would help pay for cleaner technology and discourage some additional flying, rather than passing all the costs to taxpayers.

chapters.title: Farming, forests and the uncertain role of carbon removal
chapters.takeaway: Farmers need stable support to change land use, while the Government must explain how its ambitious carbon removal plans will work if it chooses to reduce emissions more slowly elsewhere.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: Emissions from farming and land use have barely fallen since 2008. The Government has published new land use and farming plans. Will they finally give farmers enough certainty to make substantial changes?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: There are encouraging developments. The Government has set out guidance for land use and funding for farming improvements, with environmental farming support expected to reach around £2 billion a year by 2029. But the land use guidance isn't compulsory, and funding certainty stops around 2030. Planting trees or restoring peatland requires support over much longer periods. Annual tree planting needs to rise from just over 15,000 hectares in 2024-25 to more than 35,000 by 2030.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: What would make that increase possible? Tree planting is largely managed by the different UK nations, so isn't the situation different across the country?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Yes, and those differences show how strongly funding affects results. Tree planting fell in Scotland after support changed. In England, planting has risen for several years as payments improved and applications became easier. Farmers and landowners need stable, long-term financial incentives. Without them, we can't expect people to commit land and money to these projects.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: Should Government set a formal target for reducing cattle and sheep numbers? Livestock produces substantial emissions, but reducing UK farming might also encourage imports produced elsewhere.

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Our modelling assumes fewer livestock, partly because existing eating habits and farming patterns are already changing. Cattle numbers fell by about 1% and sheep by 2% last year, while household beef and lamb purchases fell 5% in 2025. These changes aren't necessarily caused by climate policy. The Government has chosen not to rely significantly on livestock reductions in its plan, and that's its decision.

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Our approach looks at the whole area of land available. If fewer animals need grazing space, some land can be used for trees and peatland restoration, potentially creating alternative income for farmers. If Government chooses a different approach, it needs to explain where that land will come from and how it will pay for other ways of reducing emissions. Supporting farming communities through changing markets is important whichever route it chooses.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: We've also had serious wildfires following very wet and then very dry weather. Are their emissions significant, and should future farming policies help people choose vegetation that's less vulnerable to fire?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Wildfires are likely to become more frequent as the climate changes. The emissions from forest fires were around 0.1 million tonnes of carbon dioxide in 2024, relatively small compared with other sources, but potentially increasing. Farmers are also already facing heat, drought and changing growing seasons. They've asked us for more guidance on what to plant and how to manage land as these risks grow. We need to consider that alongside emissions reduction.

turns.speaker: John Whitby
turns.text: The Government has responded to Alan Whitehead's review of greenhouse gas removal. How confident are you in its approach, and how urgently does it need a proper plan?

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: Removing carbon dioxide will be necessary, but we favour reducing emissions directly wherever that's practical and affordable. The Government is relying more heavily on engineered removals than we recommend. In our assessment, 94% of the removals it expects are backed by plans that either have significant risks or lack enough detail. It urgently needs a clear delivery plan, regular progress checks and alternatives if technologies develop more slowly than expected. Aligning that with its next carbon budget plan would make sense.

turns.speaker: John Whitby
turns.text: Given that the world has already experienced warming above 1.5°C, is 2050 still the right date for reaching net zero? And should the Government explain carbon removal technologies more clearly to the public?

turns.speaker: Dr Eoin Devane
turns.text: Every additional amount of warming matters, and our assessment remains that reaching net zero carbon dioxide emissions around mid-century, alongside major cuts in other greenhouse gases, is consistent with the scientific evidence. The public doesn't necessarily need to understand every removal technology. But if taxpayers are funding them, Government should explain the costs and benefits. Communities where facilities are proposed must also be consulted properly, with their concerns heard and addressed wherever possible.
